item: One robots entry, one schedule stamp and one politeness interval per host, whatever userinfo a URL carries and however its host and port are spelled; the userinfo masked in the activity monitor and in the URL logs outside the fetcher (R621)
summary: R621, OPEN_QUEUE item 46 (the leftovers R620 named), three parts in one PR, with the folds of two security reads (Steward 3: GO with items 1 to 4 and 8; an independent read: GO with S1, N1, N2, N4 and a NaN edge). It ships after R620 and R622, both taken in by merge. (1) ONE ENTRY PER HOST. BEFORE: the fetcher keyed every per-host record by scheme://netloc and netloc as WRITTEN (src/ingest/__init__.py, fetch() and declared_sitemaps()). So http://alice:pw@host/a and http://host/b were two hosts. Measured with the real EthicalFetcher against a 127.0.0.1 server: two robots.txt reads, the first sending the credentials as Basic auth (the robots URL was built from that key); two entries in robots_cache.json and in host_schedule.json, the user name and password written to disk; two politeness intervals (_last_request); two per-host locks; two Tor circuits, the stream-isolation SOCKS user name being the netloc with its punctuation taken out, so the password reached the proxy. Likewise HOST.Example, host:, host:080, host:80 and https://host:443 were each a host of their own, each with its own robots read, interval, lock and circuit (Steward 3's item 2), so a feed linking one site two ways doubled its rate. NOW: one helper, _host_netloc(netloc, scheme), gives the HOST KEY: the userinfo out (everything up to the LAST @); the host as urllib.parse reads it (.hostname, lower-cased: the name the SSRF guard checks), an IPv6 literal back in its brackets; the port as its number, with leading zeros, an empty port and the scheme's default port gone (80 for http, 443 for https). In host_schedule.json, which records no scheme, every explicit port stays: host:443 is also the key of http://host:443. A TRAILING DOT STAYS. This is the brief's stop clause, agreed with the coordinator: news.example. is an absolute name, and news.example a relative one that the resolver can complete through resolv.conf's search list (first under ndots above one, as in containers; after an NXDOMAIN under the default), so the two can be two hosts. RFC 3986 equivalence does not fold the dot either. Both parsers keep it, so the guard checks the dotted name, and a key without it would send the robots read to a name the guard never checked, or hand one name's robots answer and backoff to the other. WHERE THE KEY IS USED: the robots decision, cause and failure count; the schedule stamp; the interval; the host lock; and the Tor circuit, in fetch() and declared_sitemaps(). Both take it AFTER R622's _refuse_parser_mismatch, which reads the URL as written and refuses any urllib3/urlparse disagreement first. crawl_delay_for and forget_robots read the cache through it, per scheme. _guarded_redirect_get's fallback mapping, which the preflights reach, builds the circuit from it (Steward 3's item 3; it passed the raw netloc to the Tor isolation user name). CHECKED: 53,760 spelled URLs and 200,000 random authorities. Among those _refuse_parser_mismatch accepts, the robots URL built from the key reaches the same host and effective port as the page URL for urlparse and for urllib3, no key holds an @, and no key is shared by two different (scheme, host, port). The two persistence-failure DEBUG lines (R620's failure_url / failure_netloc wiring kept) and the clock-corrected-stamp INFO line therefore write the host only. THE ROBOTS READ goes to the page URL's scheme, host and port without the credentials: one anonymous read per host is what one entry per host means. A host whose robots.txt itself needs a login answers 401/403 and is refused (fail-closed, cause refused). When the page URL carried userinfo, that refusal now ends in the fixed words '(robots.txt is read without the page address's credentials)' (the independent read's N2). The sentence before them is unchanged, and every reader the R620 site tests use classifies it as it classifies the plain refusal. The page request still sends the credentials. A backslash before the @ is refused by R622's _refuse_parser_mismatch before any request, the robots read's included. (1b) AT LOAD. WHICH KEYS: an older build's keys that are not host keys, credentialed or spelled otherwise, leave both files and memory, whatever OO_ROBOTS_CACHE_PERSIST and OO_HOST_SCHEDULE_PERSIST say (Steward 3's item 4). With persistence off nothing new is written: a file is rewritten only when it holds such a key, atomically under its lock, with only what it already held. The four loaders and the two writers leave such keys out. ROBOTS: robots_cache.json's are DROPPED. An entry is a cache whose absence costs one robots.txt read, and a decision read WITH the credentials is not the anonymous answer the host's one entry holds. SCHEDULE: host_schedule.json's are MERGED into the host key's. This is a DELIBERATE READING of the ruling's 'drop': the credentialed key IS dropped and only its wait is kept, the later not_before and the larger delay_s winning whichever key held them. That never weakens politeness: a stamp is the host's own stated wish and lapses by time alone. A non-finite or unreadable stamp counts as absent, so a NaN clean stamp no longer makes the credentialed wait disappear (the independent read's NaN edge). Because the file records no scheme, the loader also LENDS each bare host:80 and host:443 stamp to host in memory, keeping it under its own key, so an older build's https://host:443 stamp still holds for https://host. The cost, stated: host also waits out an http://host:443 or https://host:80 stamp. (2) THE ACTIVITY MONITOR (ActivityMonitor.fetch_started) kept the raw URL and its netloc. They are served by /api/system/vitals: the top bar shows _shortUrl(current_fetch.url), and the task manager's per-source rates row is per_host_rates[].host. The URL slot is now failure_url(url). The host slot is the fetcher's own host key (the independent read's N4), so one host is one rate row, credentials or spelling aside. It is imported on use and never raises: on any error, or a host urllib.parse cannot read, it falls back to the masked netloc, then '?'. No UI script needed a change. (3) URL LOGS OUTSIDE THE FETCHER write the URL through failure_url, imported on use because a top-level import would load src.ingest into every keyword pass: duckduckgo.py fifteen; url_utils.py three (canonicalize, domain, base URL); security.py two (sanitize_url, safe_href); link_analyzer/extractor.py four. And three more from the fold: duckduckgo find_missing_rss_feeds's two lines that name a source's domain (S1). _extract_domain fills that domain with a netloc, userinfo included, and failure_url missed it because it has no //. A new _logged_domain masks up to and including its LAST @ and writes the rest through failure_netloc. batch.py's redo WARNING (N1), which wrote e.requested_url raw. It now writes failure_url, and the URL's userinfo_secrets go to log_failure, because a database error can quote the row's parameters. TESTS: tests/test_host_key_userinfo_r621.py, 73 cases (33 before the fold). The spelling variants share one key, one robots read, one interval, one lock and one circuit, and a different host or port (the trailing dot included) never shares a key. Spelled keys are dropped or merged at load, in the loaders and in the writers, and a bare default-port stamp is lent. A merge where the PLAIN stamp is the later one keeps it (max, not 'the credentialed key wins'). NaN, inf, text and missing clean stamps. A credentialed page whose robots.txt answers 401 is refused, and the robots request carried no Authorization. The scrub with each persist flag off, and its control. The fallback circuit; the N2 caveat with its readers and its two controls; one rate row and the monitor's fallback; S1 and N1. On the pre-fold head 159c2c253, 39 of the 73 fail. tests/test_failure_url_sites_r620.py's robots-unavailable case expects the bare host, since the key holds no userinfo. MUTANTS: 48 on R621, all killed. 38 on the fold, all killed: each key part undone (the identity, the default port kept, zeros kept, an empty port kept, no lower-casing, no brackets), the dot stripped, each site without the scheme or raw, each normal form put back to the @ test, the merge made a drop or 'the non-normal key wins', the lend removed or moving its key or overwriting the host's own stamp, the fallback raw, each scrub behind its flag or rewriting every file, each finiteness check, the caveat removed, unconditional or for any cause, the monitor slot masked or raising, each duckduckgo line raw, the mask up to the first @, failure_netloc or the guard removed, the batch URL raw or without its secrets, and R622's call removed from fetch(). NOT CHANGED, NAMED. Data handed back to a caller, not masked: duckduckgo _extract_domain's result domain (the netloc with its userinfo); url_utils.canonicalize_url's canonical_url (Article.canonical_url); Article.url, which stores the URL as given; the link records, which keep an article's links as written; FetchResult.requested_url and final_url; scheduler/runlog.export_delta's url and canonical_url columns, written to a plaintext export. Also an exception's own text: urllib.parse's NFKC netloc check names the netloc, and log_failure writes that line by design. Found and left: api/jobs _live_fetch passes the snapshot's current_fetch dict to urlparse, so that job's label is always 'fetch in flight'. FOLLOW-UPS: R624, its own PR after R621: src/ingest/crawl.py:114 _registrable_host splits on ':' before the '@', so https://good.example:x@evil.example/ reads as good.example and same_domain_only (crawl.py, sitemap.py) follows it; robots, SSRF and politeness still apply to evil.example. Recorded with no PR: _with_stream_isolation cuts the Tor isolation token to 32 characters (src/safety/fetcher.py:348), so hosts sharing a 32-character prefix share a circuit; and moving failure_url to a leaf module. Release-notes line: Credentials written into a page address no longer appear in the robots cache, the host schedule, the task manager's host slot or the logs. The robots.txt request no longer sends them either, so a site whose robots.txt itself needs a login is now treated as disallowing collection. A site written with different capitals or its default port now gets one robots.txt read and one politeness wait. (R621)
